subject: English
description: Masculine, feminine, common, neuter genders; pairs

questions.explanation: NEPHEW (m) ↔ NIECE (f). Other key gender pairs: BROTHER-SISTER, FATHER-MOTHER, UNCLE-AUNT, COUSIN (common), GRANDFATHER-GRANDMOTHER, SON-DAUGHTER, BOY-GIRL, KING-QUEEN, PRINCE-PRINCESS, ACTOR-ACTRESS (some forms now considered dated; modern English uses 'actor' for both), WAITER-WAITRESS, HERO-HEROINE, GOD-GODDESS, LANDLORD-LANDLADY, BACHELOR-SPINSTER, MONK-NUN, BULL-COW, COCK-HEN, HORSE-MARE, LION-LIONESS, TIGER-TIGRESS. INSIGHT — modern trend is GENDER-NEUTRAL forms: ACTOR (for any gender), CHAIR / CHAIRPERSON (vs chairman), POLICE OFFICER (vs policeman), FIREFIGHTER, SERVER (vs waiter/waitress).

questions.explanation: WIDOW (f, woman whose husband died) ↔ WIDOWER (m, man whose wife died). Both retain marital identity; second marriage possible. BACHELOR ↔ SPINSTER (or 'unmarried woman' — modern preferred). ANIMAL gender pairs are useful too: BULL-COW (cattle), STALLION-MARE (horses), DRAKE-DUCK, GANDER-GOOSE, RAM-EWE (sheep), BUCK-DOE (deer), STAG-HIND, BULL-COW (elephant + whale + many large animals). YOUNG: calf (cow), foal (horse), lamb (sheep), kid (goat), piglet, puppy, kitten. COLLECTIVE NOUNS: pride of lions, herd of cattle, flock of sheep, school of fish, swarm of bees, pack of wolves.
questions.subject: English

questions.explanation: DUKE ↔ DUCHESS. NOBILITY hierarchy (UK): KING/QUEEN > PRINCE/PRINCESS > DUKE/DUCHESS > MARQUESS/MARCHIONESS > EARL/COUNTESS > VISCOUNT/VISCOUNTESS > BARON/BARONESS. BARONET-BARONETESS. KNIGHT-DAME. SAME PREFIXES different: SIR (knight-male) / DAME (knight-female; 'Lady' colloquially). EMPEROR-EMPRESS, CZAR-CZARINA (Russia). Other suffixes: −ESS (most common: actress, princess); −INE (heroine — old form); −ETTE (suffragette). MANY −ESS / −INE forms are now CONSIDERED OUTDATED in modern English (use neutral form). Notable EXCEPTIONS still in use: WAITRESS (sometimes), ACTRESS (often), GODDESS, EMPRESS.

questions.explanation: BACHELOR ↔ SPINSTER (formal); 'BACHELORETTE' is colloquial/American. Note 'spinster' has dated, sometimes pejorative connotation in modern English; many prefer simply 'unmarried woman' or 'single woman'. INSIGHT — language evolves; some traditional gender pairs feel awkward today. Modern English moves toward GENDER-NEUTRAL or GENDER-AVOIDING. FOR PYQ EXAMS: still tested in classical pair form; learn pairs. OTHER USEFUL PAIRS: hero-heroine; bridegroom-bride; god-goddess; benefactor-benefactress (rare); poet-poetess (poetess now considered dated; just 'poet'); host-hostess; tailor-seamstress; instructor-instructress (rare).
questions.subject: English

questions.explanation: GOOSE (f) ↔ GANDER (m). DUCK (f) ↔ DRAKE (m). Bird gender pairs: hen-cock (rooster); peahen-peacock; swan-cob (male swan = cob; cygnet = young). MAMMAL pairs: cow-bull (cattle); mare-stallion (horse); doe-buck (deer/rabbit); ewe-ram (sheep); nanny-billy (goat); sow-boar (pig); jenny-jack (donkey); vixen-fox; tigress-tiger; lioness-lion. ELEPHANT pair = cow-bull. WHALE = cow-bull. Same applies: dolphins, deer, etc. KEY EXAMPLES of NEUTER: chair, table, book, machine — gender-less. COMMON GENDER: child, baby, doctor, teacher, friend, leader, citizen — used for either sex.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Which of the following is COMMON GENDER (used for both sexes)?
questions.explanation: FOUR GENDERS in English: (1) MASCULINE (boy, son, brother, king); (2) FEMININE (girl, daughter, sister, queen); (3) COMMON (used for both sexes — child, baby, friend, doctor, teacher, leader, citizen, neighbour, parent, MP, student, professor, engineer, manager); (4) NEUTER (no sex — book, table, chair, plant, sun, river, idea, courage). ENGLISH grammatical gender is REAL-WORLD-BASED (mostly). Compare HINDI / FRENCH / GERMAN where every noun has grammatical gender (table = la table = feminine in French; der Tisch = masculine in German). PERSONIFICATION often gives gender: SHIPS feminine ('she'); COUNTRIES feminine ('she'); SUN often masculine, MOON feminine (literary).

questions.explanation: AUTHOR (m or generic) ↔ AUTHORESS (f, but DATED — modern English uses 'AUTHOR' for any gender). Same trend: ACTOR (preferred over actress for both genders in many publications); POET (over poetess); SCULPTOR (over sculptress); EDITOR (over editress, never used); PROFESSOR (gender-neutral). MODERN STYLE GUIDES (AP, Reuters, NYT) increasingly avoid feminine -ess suffix. STILL standard in: WAITRESS, STEWARDESS (though now 'flight attendant' more common), GODDESS. JOURNALISTIC AVOIDANCE: 'female author' / 'woman writer' if gender info needed (rather than 'authoress').
